bib.title: Towards AI-Complete Question Answering: A Set of Prerequisite Toy Tasks
bib.venue: Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2016 (arXiv v10, 31 Dec 2015)

question: Can a set of 20 simple, automatically generated question-answering tasks, each testing one reasoning skill, expose which capabilities current learning systems lack on the way to text understanding?
hypothesis: Performing well on all 20 tasks is a prerequisite for any system aiming at full text understanding and reasoning; failing any one implies likely failure on real-world tasks needing the same skill.
contributions: A set of 20 toy QA tasks (bAbI) generated from a text-adventure-like simulation, each isolating one skill
Benchmark results for N-gram, LSTM, Memory Network and structured SVM baselines
Extensions to Memory Networks: adaptive memory (variable hops, multi-word answers), N-gram features, nonlinear matching
Public release of data and generator code, plus Hindi and shuffled-word versions

method.summary: Twenty tasks are generated by a simulation of actors and objects moving among locations; a simple grammar renders statements and questions with synonyms and the true answers come from the simulation state. Each task has 1000 training and 1000 test questions, and models are scored by test accuracy with a pass threshold of 95%. Baselines (N-gram classifier, LSTM, Memory Networks, structured SVM with coreference and SRL features) are compared with the authors' extended Memory Networks.
method.task: synthetic reading-comprehension question answering (single-word or word-list answers)

datasets.name: bAbI 20 tasks (English)
datasets.size: 1000 training questions and 1000 test questions per task; 20 tasks
datasets.split: 1000 train / 1000 test per task; also trained jointly on all tasks
datasets.source: Generated by simulation; http://fb.ai/babi, code at github.com/facebook/bAbI-tasks
datasets.preprocessing: Simple grammar with verb/object/actor synonyms; vocabulary about 150 words; typically 4 actors, 6 locations, 3 objects per task

datasets.name: bAbI Hindi and shuffled-English versions
datasets.source: released with the data; not evaluated in this paper
datasets.preprocessing: shuffled English words are unreadable by humans

models.name: N-gram classifier
models.architecture: linear classifier on bag-of-N-grams of story sentences sharing at least one word with the question

models.name: LSTM
models.architecture: reads the story to the question then outputs an answer

models.name: MemNN (Weston et al. 2014)
models.architecture: Memory Network, k=2 hops, bag-of-words embedding match s(x,y)=Phi_x(x)^T U^T U Phi_y(y), D=3|W|, write-time features

models.name: MemNN AM+NG+NL
models.architecture: MemNN with adaptive memory (variable hops until STOP fact, max 10 loops, multi-word answers via w-null), bag of 3-grams (N=1,2,3 in appendix), and tanh 2-layer nonlinear matching E(x)=tanh(W tanh(Phi_x(x)^T U))

other.variants: AM, AM+NG, AM+NL, AM+NG+NL, AM+multilinear (position-binned P_sz maps, mean 93)

models.name: Structured SVM with COREF+SRL features
models.architecture: cascade: Stanford coreference replaces mentions, SENNA SRL, ranking of at most 3 supporting facts with exhaustive search over a pruned set, then a response-stage SVM
models.init_from: external labeled data (Stanford coref, SENNA SRL)

training.objective: answer prediction; for strongly supervised models also supporting-fact selection (MemNN trained with SGD on both)
training.optimizer: inferred: stochastic gradient descent, stated for the MemNN only

other.hyperparameter_selection: Learning rates and other hyperparameters for all methods are chosen using the training set

inference.decoding: MemNN: argmax over supporting facts then argmax over dictionary words (iterated until null word for multi-word answers)
inference.samples: single run per cell; no seeds or variance reported
inference.retrieval: MemNN retrieves k supporting memories from the story (k=2 original; adaptive up to 10)

metrics.name: test accuracy
metrics.definition: fraction of the 1000 test questions answered exactly right per task; a task is passed at >=95%

metrics.name: examples required for >=95%
metrics.definition: smallest training-set size reaching 95% for MemNN AM+NG+NL, FAIL if not reached within 1000

eval.protocol: Three tracks: weakly supervised (answers only), strongly supervised (supporting facts at train time only), external resources. A single model should be evaluated across all tasks without per-task tuning (the paper's recommendation); main table trains per task, last column trains on all tasks jointly.

evidence.quote: For each task we use 1000 questions for training, and 1000 for testing, and report the test accuracy.
Learning rates and other hyperparameters for all methods are chosen using the training set.

results.claim: MemNN with adaptive memory, N-grams and nonlinearity reaches the best mean accuracy over the 20 tasks, trained per task on 1000 examples.
results.setup: bAbI 20 tasks, 1000 training examples per task, strong supervision, MemNN AM+NG+NL; baseline is original MemNN
results.table: Table 3, row Mean Performance, column MemNN AM + NG + NL (baseline column MemNN Weston et al. 2014 = 75)

results.claim: The LSTM baseline (answers only) has a mean accuracy of 49% and the N-gram classifier 34%.
results.setup: bAbI 20 tasks, 1000 training examples per task, weak supervision
results.table: Table 3, row Mean Performance, column LSTM (baseline column N-gram Classifier = 34)

results.claim: The structured SVM with coreference and SRL features and external data does not beat the extended MemNN: mean 79% and fails 9 tasks.
results.setup: bAbI 20 tasks, 1000 examples, strong supervision plus external resources
results.table: Table 3, row Mean Performance, column Structured SVM
results.quote: The structured SVM, despite having access to external resources, does not perform better, still failing at 9 tasks.
results.note: Mean 79 equals the AM-only MemNN mean.

results.claim: Extensions upgrade 9 tasks from failure to success compared with the original MemNN.
results.setup: MemNN AM+NG+NL vs original MemNN, 1000 training examples
results.quote: indeed AM+NG+NL (column 9) gives improved results over both, with a total of 9 tasks that have been upgraded from failure to success compared to the original MemNN model.

results.claim: Joint training on all tasks gives a mean of 92%, close to per-task training (93%).
results.setup: MemNN AM+NG+NL trained on all tasks at once
results.table: Table 3, row Mean Performance, column MultiTask Training

results.claim: Path finding (task 19) is the hardest: best accuracy 36% for MemNN AM+NG+NL.
results.setup: Task 19, MemNN AM+NG+NL, 1000 training examples; cannot be solved even with 10000 examples
results.table: Table 3, row 19 - Path Finding, column MemNN AM + NG + NL
results.quote: Two tasks, positional reasoning 17 and path ﬁnding 19 cannot be solved even with 10000 examples

results.claim: Most succeeding tasks need 100-500 training examples; task 8 needs 5000 and task 7 needs 10000.
results.quote: Task 8 requires 5000 examples and 7 requires 10000, hence they are labeled as FAIL.

results.claim: Original MemNN fails yes/no (task 6, 47%) because its linear scoring cannot model the three-way interaction of query, supporting fact and answer.
results.setup: Task 6, original MemNN; baseline is AM+NG+NL
results.table: Table 3, row 6 - Yes/No Questions, column MemNN Weston et al. (2014) (baseline AM+NL = 100)
results.quote: the linear scoring function of standard MemNNs cannot model the match between query, supporting fact and a yes/no answer as this requires three-way interactions.

results.claim: The vocabulary is about 150 words with typically 4 actors, 6 locations and 3 objects per task.
results.quote: the entities and the vocabulary size is small (150 words, and typically 4 actors, 6 locations and 3 objects used per task)

results.claim: The 95% pass threshold and 1000 training examples are arbitrary choices.
results.quote: The choice of 95% (and 1000 training examples) is arbitrary.

limits: Tasks are synthetic with a tiny vocabulary and short, unnested sentences; the authors say they are not a substitute for real data.
Solving the tasks does not imply real reasoning; the authors say a learner solving them is not necessarily close to full reasoning.
The MemNN results use strong supervision (supporting facts), which the authors call far stronger than is realistic.
No known general, non-hand-engineered weakly supervised method solves the tasks with 1000 examples or fewer (as of 2015).
Single reported accuracy per cell, no seeds or variance; the 95% threshold and 1000 examples are arbitrary.
Training details (learning rate, embedding size, epochs, batch size) are not given. Dated: MemN2N, DMN and later transformer models solve these tasks.
